title: Centroids, Clusters and Crime: Anchoring the Geographic Profiles of Serial Criminals

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF page 1 is the summary sheet; PDF pages 2-46 display printed pages 1-45.

notes: All pages were read in order and all page layouts were visually covered.
Gamma, kappa, theta, flowchart text, figure labels, and displayed formulas were reconciled from bounded JPEG review proxies.

context_sources.summary: Geographic-profiling literature motivates anchors and journey-to-crime patterns.
Published case-study plots provide recoverable but indirect coordinate data.
Eighteen references cover crime geography, clustering, Gamma MLE, silhouettes, and human profilers.

inputs: ordered coordinates of previous violent serial crimes
decisions: where to prioritize limited police resources
whether centroid or cluster structure has retrospective value

section_map.summary: The summary moves from geographic profiling and explicit spatial assumptions through single- and multiple-anchor predictors, retrospective effectiveness testing, observed successes, abrupt-behavior failure, and the practical preference for anchor-point prediction.
Centroids, Clusters and Crime: Anchoring the Geographic Profiles of Serial Criminals names the two technical devices, the domain, and the anchor-point mechanism.

The introduction converts an investigation anecdote into a pattern-recognition task, declares ordered crime coordinates as input, compares one- and many-anchor schemes, names the effectiveness selector, and reserves final judgment for experienced police.

The background defines geographic profiling and anchor points, contrasts global hot spots and high-dimensional offender features, and argues for a low-input individual likelihood surface grounded in journey-to-crime evidence.

The assumptions operationalize an approximately urban metric domain, dense targets, Euclidean movement, adequate extent, violent serial crime, one offender, event-merging rules, and spatial ordering instead of unreliable time intervals.

The test-set section rejects simulations that share the predictor's assumptions, reconstructs coordinates from published plots, documents source limitations, and separates development from blind examples.

The metric section turns a vivid random-baseline story into resource allocation at the held-out crime point, normalizes likelihood surfaces, defines kappa and kappa_s, and restricts cross-dataset comparisons through a standardized search domain.
The bridge section transfers mature anchor-point research to next-event prediction and announces parallel single- and multiple-anchor routes.

The centroid method builds a search square, estimates one anchor, fits a Gamma radial crater, shifts it by the most recent radial change, reports two successes and one failure, then rejects uncalibrated angular extensions.

The cluster method selects two to four centroid-linkage clusters by average silhouette, reuses the crater locally, treats singleton clusters as outliers, combines cluster surfaces by size and recency, and contrasts precision with catastrophic miss risk.

The final predictor repeatedly truncates the sequence, rejects methods that underperform a flat surface too often, selects the higher historical running mean, and labels that mean a rough confidence estimate.
The practical extensions assign map dead-zone removal and parameter judgment to an intuitive police team and compare passive next-crime patrol with active anchor-point investigation.

The conclusion recomposes assumptions, Gamma craters, clustering, three-case evidence, historical selection, confidence limits, human interpretation, and the boundary between next-crime and anchor-point prediction.
The executive summary restates inputs, assumptions, two methods, track-record selection, strengths, limitations, warnings, and the recommendation to combine the map with human judgment.
The references connect crime mapping, geographic profiling, clustering, Gamma estimation, silhouette analysis, and human geographic-profile performance.

assumptions.summary: The search region is approximately urban: potential targets are dense at block scale.
Movement is effectively uninhibited and Euclidean L2 distance represents relevant travel separation.
The search domain is large enough that prediction likelihood decays before its boundary.
The event sequence concerns violent serial assaults, rapes, or murders by one offender.
Very close events in time and space may be encoded as one event.
Spatial order is useful even when exact crime times and intervals are unreliable.
Crime locations exhibit persistent patterning around one or more daily-activity anchor points.
Observed radial distances are independent samples from one Gamma family for the fitted step.
Two to four clusters are a plausible range for significant activity anchors.
Cluster size and recent activity are useful predictors of the next active anchor.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Private police datasets are unavailable, and same-model simulation is rejected as circular.
Pixel Point Analysis digitizes published maps and rescales raster coordinates into meters.
Seven sequences are described, while only three ordered rape sequences become complete blind-test examples.
A centroid-centered square with side three times the maximum separation fixes the paper's comparison domain.

models.summary: The resource-allocation ratio interface preserves metric definition: Interpret relative preparedness at the held-out crime location.
The likelihood ratio interface preserves normalized metric: Evaluate two normalized likelihood surfaces at the observed next crime.
The flat-baseline likelihood ratio interface preserves standard metric: Compare a predictor with uniform resource allocation.
The standardized square extent interface preserves search scaling: Standardize the flat baseline area across examples.
The equal-weight centroid interface preserves centroid: Estimate the single anchor point from previous crimes.
The Euclidean radius interface preserves radial map: Map each crime coordinate to its distance from the anchor.
The Gamma density interface preserves Gamma pdf: Represent either a buffer-zone mode or monotone radial decay.
The independent likelihood interface preserves Gamma likelihood: Fit crater shape and scale from observed radii.
The log likelihood interface preserves Gamma log likelihood: Expose the numerical maximum-likelihood problem.
The conditional scale estimator interface preserves Gamma scale MLE: Estimate Gamma scale conditional on shape.
The discrete probability normalization interface preserves surface normalization: Convert the radial density to a grid likelihood surface summing to one.
The latest radial change interface preserves radial increment: Measure the most recent inward or outward radial change.
The additive radial shift interface preserves shifted radius: Shift the fitted radius distribution by the latest trend.
The expectation shift interface preserves shifted expectation: Show how the adjustment changes predicted mean radius.
The silhouette coefficient interface preserves silhouette: Score how well a point fits its current cluster relative to alternatives.
The cluster-size share interface preserves size weight: Give more influence to clusters containing more crimes.
The mean temporal-index share interface preserves recency weight: Give more influence to recently active clusters.
The normalized weighted mixture interface preserves cluster surface: Combine local crater and singleton surfaces into one prediction.
The historical mean effectiveness interface preserves running mean: Summarize retrospective next-event effectiveness through step M.
The majority underperformance rule interface preserves validity threshold: Reject a method that loses to uniform allocation in more than half the retrospective trials.
The endpoint mean comparison interface preserves method choice: Choose among methods that pass the validity rule.
The historical-effectiveness confidence interface preserves confidence proxy: Use past holdout effectiveness as a rough future-confidence proxy.
Digitize crime marks from published raster plots, rescale coordinates to meters, and retain series order.
Build the expanded domain, find one centroid, fit a Gamma radial crater, shift by the latest radial change, and normalize the surface.
For each count from two through four, merge clusters by centroid distance, compute non-singleton silhouettes, and choose the largest average.
Build one crater per multi-point cluster, one Gaussian contribution per singleton, weight by size and recency, sum, and renormalize.
Predict each event from its predecessors, count underperformance, reject invalid methods, compare running means, and report a rough confidence proxy.

dependency_graph.handoff: Recovered ordered coordinates supply the single-anchor centroid.
The estimated anchor converts locations to radii.
Observed radii supply the Gamma likelihood.
Fitted Gamma parameters supply the normalized crater surface.
The most recent radial increment shifts the prediction distribution.
The centroid surface is evaluated against the flat baseline at held-out points.
Silhouette comparison supplies the selected spatial clusters.
Size and recency components supply weights for the cluster mixture.
Selected clusters supply local crater and singleton contributions.
Centroid predictions supply one retrospective candidate to the selector.
Cluster predictions supply the second retrospective candidate.
Historical running means supply the valid-method comparison.
The selected method's running mean becomes the rough confidence proxy.

verification.summary: The authors reject same-model synthetic data and use coordinates recovered from published empirical plots.
verification.limitation: Recovered pixels still lack raw case provenance and measurement uncertainty.

verification.summary: The search square is standardized before comparing effectiveness across three complete examples.
verification.strength: Makes the flat baseline more comparable within the paper.
verification.limitation: The factor three and claimed coverage are not empirically calibrated.

verification.summary: Each case removes the chronologically last crime and evaluates the fitted surface at that held-out point.
verification.strength: Preserves temporal order and a genuine held-out location.
verification.limitation: Only one final event per example is used in the first comparison.

verification.summary: Centroid results report kappa_s=12.19, 12.15, and 0.38 for C, B, and A.
verification.strength: Includes two successes and an explicit failure.
verification.limitation: Three selected sequences cannot establish statistical significance.

verification.summary: Average silhouette compares two, three, and four clusters after excluding singleton contributions.
verification.strength: Uses one data-derived comparison instead of fixing every dataset to four clusters.
verification.limitation: The search cap and singleton convention influence the choice.

verification.summary: Cluster results report kappa_s=15.82, 22.95, and about 0.001.
verification.strength: Shows sharper predictions can improve or catastrophically harm the score.
verification.limitation: The same small recovered corpus supports both design and evaluation discussion.

verification.summary: Truncated histories predict each next event and form eventwise and running-mean effectiveness curves.
verification.strength: Uses more than the last event and gates methods that often lose to uniform allocation.
verification.limitation: No independent corpus calibrates the rejection threshold or confidence meaning.

verification.summary: Projected means C=6.65, B=8.473, A=12.25 are compared with final outcomes 15.82, 22.95, 0.001.
verification.strength: Displays the proxy beside outcomes instead of hiding the severe miss.
verification.limitation: Offender A demonstrates that the proxy is not calibrated confidence.

results_trace.summary: Offender C centroid kappa_s=12.19; its next crime lies near the crater maximum.
Offender B centroid kappa_s=12.15 and Offender A centroid kappa_s=0.38.
Cluster predictions yield C=15.82, B=22.95, and A approximately 0.001.
The combined algorithm selects clustering for all three cases, but projected confidence fails badly for A.

contributions.summary: Defines an operational resource-allocation multiplier at a held-out event.
Uses one fitted Gamma family to span buffer-zone and monotone radial patterns.
Adds data-selected multiple anchors through hierarchical clustering and silhouettes.
Uses rolling historical next-event performance to reject or select predictors.
Explicitly positions the model as an augmentation to local police knowledge.

writing_logic.summary: Summary chain: task -> assumptions -> one anchor -> many anchors -> holdout metric -> outcomes -> failure and practical boundary.
Introduction chain: investigation story -> pattern-recognition abstraction -> input/output -> parallel methods -> effectiveness selector -> human handoff.
Assumption chain: domain label -> checkable spatial condition -> empirical rationale -> police interpretation boundary.
Data chain: unavailable sources -> reject circular simulation -> recover published plots -> declare blind examples.
Metric chain: weak random baseline -> operational preparedness -> normalized ratio -> flat comparison -> domain dependence.
Model chain: inherited anchor evidence -> centroid crater -> multi-anchor clusters -> retrospective selector.
Decision chain: abstract surface -> local dead-zone and parameter judgment -> patrol versus anchor investigation.

language_observations.summary: A narrative opening is converted into a mathematical pattern-recognition contract.
Competing approaches are dismissed through task fit and data burden before the retained low-input design.
Broad assumptions become enumerated spatial tests and explicit human responsibilities.
A favorable metric is immediately bounded by domain-size dependence and low sample count.
Two successes are followed by a named failure rather than a universal robustness claim.
Precision-risk tradeoff is made memorable through controlled metaphors such as gamble and cluster luck.
Evidence suggests without proving marks a deliberate claim-strength boundary.
Executive bullets pair strengths with equally prominent operational limitations.

visualization_observations.summary: Compresses assumptions, both predictors, the retrospective test, empirical outcomes, and practical boundaries.
Confirms the complete chapter route and the late placement of conclusions and executive guidance.
Pairs a published Offender B map with pixel-extracted coordinates to document the data-recovery interface.
Shows the single-anchor search-domain, centroid, crater, temporal adjustment, and output sequence.
Contrasts two Gamma parameter regimes to justify one family for buffer zones and monotone decay.
Illustrates a crater fitted to the Peter Sutcliffe sequence.
Links Offender C's heat map and surface plot to kappa_s=12.19 and patrol-area waste.
Links Offender B's centroid heat map and surface to anisotropy and a source label error.
Shows the Offender A outlier failure under the centroid method.
Shows the cluster-selection, local-centroid, crater, weighting, temporal, and combination loop.
Displays the Offender B centroid-linkage dendrogram used before silhouette selection.
Connects average silhouette by cluster count to the resulting four spatial clusters.
Shows the Offender C cluster prediction and exposes inconsistent panel labeling.
Shows the sharper Offender B cluster prediction associated with kappa_s about 22.95.
Shows the near-zero Offender A cluster effectiveness and exposes an offender label error.
Contrasts running mean and eventwise effectiveness for centroid and cluster models.
Juxtaposes historical confidence proxies with final observed multipliers for C, B, and A.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The summary's full task-to-boundary chain plausibly improves evaluator traceability without proving validity.
Reporting a clear failure plausibly improves credibility because it exposes model scope.
A concrete human-model deployment boundary plausibly strengthens practical relevance.

weaknesses.summary: The event-merging rule calls p>0.01 highly statistically significant; the inequality conflicts with the usual small-p convention.
The summary says seven data sets from three criminals, the test-set prose says seven different criminals, and later evaluation says only three complete test data sets.
The flat-baseline multiplier depends on search area and grid definition, so its magnitude is not an invariant measure of practical value.
The three-times search-square rule and more-than-90-percent coverage claim are not estimated or uncertainty-checked on the recovered data.
The Gamma MLE prose asks for r-hat and maximization over theta and r even though the defined parameters are k and theta; the numerical parameter should be k-hat.
The temporal adjustment uses only the last radial difference, with no smoothing, uncertainty, or test that the apparent trend persists.
Figure 6(b) labels an Offender B surface as Offender C.
Singleton silhouettes are described as one and then removed from the average; this differs from common zero/undefined conventions and favors the chosen handling.
The cluster loop first requires more than two points for the centroid method but later refers to more than one, leaving two-point clusters unspecified.
A singleton Gaussian is centered on the outlier but its mean is also said to be set by a Gamma expectation; the intended width parameter is not defined.
Cluster size and recency weight components are named but the paper does not state whether they are multiplied, added, or rescaled.
Figure 12(b) says Offender S and Centroid Model while the figure caption identifies Offender C cluster output.
Figure 14(b) says Offender B while the page and caption concern Offender A; cluster captions also describe centroid-labeled panels.
The projected-versus-observed comparison table gives both numeric columns the same kappa_s header.
Historical mean effectiveness is used as confidence even though Offender A has projected 12.25 and observed 0.001, demonstrating severe outlier sensitivity.
The quadrature argument for crime-point uncertainty assumes error structure and independence that the paper does not estimate.
The executive summary claims no arbitrary parameters despite the factor-three domain, two-to-four cluster cap, half-failure rule, and unspecified weight combination.
Reference 11 visually prints 'In 1005 UK Crime Mapping Conference, 2005,' an apparent bibliographic year/title error.

independent_extensions.summary: Rebuild evaluation from released geocoded sequences with coordinate, linkage, and event-order uncertainty.
Fit radial mixture and nonparametric baselines with optimizer diagnostics and posterior predictive checks.
Compare cluster counts including one under resampling-stable criteria rather than a fixed two-to-four cap.
Specify and tune singleton kernels and size-recency combination on nested rolling holdouts.
Calibrate the historical effectiveness proxy against future outcomes and report intervals, Brier-style calibration, and catastrophic-miss risk.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain problem-pipeline-evidence-boundary summaries, parallel method contrast, and success-then-caveat routines
retain the anchor evidence to centroid to clusters to retrospective selection organization chain
retain the rejection of circular simulation while adding digitization and linkage uncertainty requirements
retain explicit metric units, spatial mechanism, domain, parameter estimation, and baseline comparisons
retain rolling-origin next-event tests and separate apparent success from external validation
treat the historical effectiveness mean as an uncalibrated proxy until independently tested
bind maps, surfaces, dendrograms, silhouette plots, and outcome tables to explicit analytical questions
retain limited-resource interpretation and the human override for dead zones and local intelligence
compare centroid and cluster variants under one search domain, holdout rule, and effectiveness definition
